item.title: Precious metals?
item.content:encoded: I don't mean to nitpick, but I think there's a minor typo/error in detailing what metal the owl spit back up. It says "indium," but indium is not a precious metal. It's somewhat rare, but it's too soft for most practical applications. (You can cut it with a knife, for instance.) Iridium, on the other hand, is a precious metal in the platinum metal group. Is that the one you meant? If not, that's fine, but it does create a minor inconsistency with the description. And since it's the only metal used as an example, it makes the discrepancy somewhat more glaring.

item.title: Re: Willing Suspension of Disbelief? Nope.
item.content:encoded:
Points (mostly) conceded.

The direct text from the article states "SCP-391 was acquired in 20██, after Park Ranger █████ ████████ reported finding nuggets of gold resembling owl pellets." and then goes on to mention that the Foundation tagged all owls within a 50 km radius, and had to release at least 100 of the tagged birds before finding the one that made the things.

I don't understand how that relates to the Ranger reporting/not reporting the gold pellets, BUT…

Also, we're just given a plural in regards to how many gold pellets the ranger found. That can be anywhere from 2 or more. Also, the report seems to have been in routine records, as opposed to being made verbally to a supervisor, so for all we know, maybe the guy got to keep what he found.

I hadn't thought of that. It's also possible the ranger helped himself to a bunch of gold pellets before he decided to report them. That explanation allows me to retain at least some of my negative view of humanity. :-)

I've also promised myself I won't post after more than two glasses of wine, ever again.

item.title: I like it.
item.content:encoded:
Articles are supposed to be a SNAPSHOT of a point in time, so not every idea will be carried out to it's fullest over time.

So the breeding experiment request in limbo is perfectly correct, and the fact the request was made (an obvious thought - if it does breed true, you have to look for more of these in the wild) makes me happy.

The metals/ingested log/requests for further experiments - there's been a lot of calls for this over the years… and the document DOES indicate the tests were performed at some point, or they wouldn't KNOW the output varies specifically with the input…

There's 4 possible ways to address it, or it can be left (unsatisfyingly) as it is now…
1. Change the FIRST citation, to say that testing is undergoing to SEE if varying input flesh produces a consistent variance in output.
2. Actually write up such experiment logs.
3. Produce a summarized list of a few critters/metals, and note that further testing is proceeding.
4. State that the records are available in document XXX-BLAH-391-Alpha. …note that you don't actually have to WRITE the document, just say that's where the information is. :)

If you do produce testing logs, I have a test idea.
White Rat/Rat = Iridium. What about a rat that has itself ingested some, oh, gold already? Does it produce both metals? More iridium? An alloy? Does the gold vanish?

item.content:encoded: This makes my inner ornithophile happy. However, 20 g is way small for either brown rats (Rattus norvegicus) or black rats (R. rattus), which average at least ten times that mass. 20 g would be good for a house mouse (Mus musculus), but I imagine Midas would have eaten those before, meaning indium would have already been found in the wild. Gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus) are somewhat more massive than mice, and golden hamsters (Mesocricetus auratus) are a bit heavier still, but I reckon either of these would work with some slight adjustments to mass. [/taxonomy nerd]
